extracted.intended_audience: aspiring novelists; students and practitioners of fiction
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for writing and evaluating novels focused on three central devices: characterization (flat vs round), point of view (narrative stance and shifts), and plot (causality, mystery, economy, and endings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Round vs flat characters
rubrics_metrics.description: The test of a round character is whether it is capable of surprising in a convincing way. If it never surprises, it is flat. If it does not convince, it is a flat pretending to be round.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Round characters have the 'incalculability of life' and can expand and contract within a book; flat characters are simple and readily reintroduced. Small, well-chosen details can modulate a character from flat into round (example: a brief sentence enlarging Lady Bertram into a rounder presence). Examples of round characters: principal characters in War and Peace, Dostoevsky's characters, parts of Proust, Madame Bovary, Becky and Beatrix (Thackeray), Parson Adams (Fielding), Lucy Snowe (Charlotte Brontë). Examples of flat characters: Henry Tilney, Mr Woodhouse, Charlotte Lucas. The novelist achieves realism by using both kinds alone or in combination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Point of view (narrator's stance and shifts)
rubrics_metrics.description: The novelist may describe characters from outside (impartial/partial onlooker), assume omniscience, place the narrator as one of the characters (limited perspective), or adopt intermediate attitudes; he may shift among these.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Point of view is a major technical device: it governs method but is not reducible to formulae. Shifting viewpoints can work if the writer can 'bounce' the reader into acceptance (examples: Dickens' Bleak House, Tolstoy's War and Peace). Excessive self-consciousness about method (Gide) weakens emotional impact. The power to adopt or shift viewpoint should be used for effect, but shifts must be convincing to readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bounce the reader (authorial persuasive authority)
rubrics_metrics.description: The central power in fiction is the writer's ability to 'bounce' the reader into accepting what he says — this is imperative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This persuasive authority can make logical incoherence acceptable to readers (example: Dickens' varying omniscience in Bleak House). It is the operative centre of method; critics may object to technical problems, but readers follow if bounced effectively. Cultivate the ability to command reader acceptance across changes of method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid authorial intimacy about individual characters
rubrics_metrics.description: It is usually dangerous for the writer to take the reader into his confidence about individual characters; this tends to cause a drop in emotional temperature and to facetiousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorial asides about characters lead to 'bar-parlour chattiness' that breaks illusion and invites analysis of the novelist's mind rather than the characters (examples: certain passages in Fielding and Thackeray). By contrast, generalizing about conditions of life or the universe (as Hardy or Conrad sometimes do) is less harmful. Keep confidences about individuals to a minimum to preserve illusion and nobility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Access to the secret life / interiority
rubrics_metrics.description: The novelist has the privilege of accessing the characters' secret life and subconscious; he can present self-communings and the inner causes of action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use interiority to show subconscious processes and how they short-circuit into action; but be mindful of standpoint and convincingness — readers only care whether the presentation of interiority is convincing, not the technical legalities of how the writer knew it. Interior access distinguishes the novel from the drama.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot as causality (definition & distinction from story)
rubrics_metrics.description: A plot is a narrative of events with the emphasis on causality (asks 'why?'); a story is narrative arranged in time sequence (asks 'and then?').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A plot suspends mere sequence to reveal causes (example formula: 'The king died, and then the queen died of grief'). Plots demand intelligence and memory from readers and can develop complex forms (mysteries, denouements). Authors should craft causality so readers can follow and eventually appreciate the 'aesthetically compact' result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mystery / detective element
rubrics_metrics.description: Mystery is essential to a plot: a suspension of time-sequence creating a 'pocket in time' whose meaning often only becomes clear pages later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mystery provides surprise and forward momentum but requires the reader's intelligence to appreciate it; it may occur crudely ('Why did the queen die?') or subtly (half-explained gestures or words whose significance dawns later). Use concealment and delayed revelation judiciously (example: Meredith's concealment of Laetitia's change in The Egoist).

rubrics_metrics.name: Expectations of reader intelligence and memory
rubrics_metrics.description: A plot presupposes an intelligent reader with memory who can hold facts, relate them, and rearrange them as the narrative proceeds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers should be given cross-correspondences and clues that accumulate; do not rely solely on curiosity ('and then — and then —'). Avoid misleading the reader; leave no loose ends and ensure that earlier details can be recalled and reinterpreted to form the final sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy and organic construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Every action or word in a plot ought to count; the narrative should be economical, spare, organic, and free from dead matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid extraneous scenes or filler; even when complex, the plot should not mislead. The ideal plot produces an organic unity where clues and causes cohere into a satisfying whole that might, in theory, have been shown at once but becomes beautiful through arrangement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauty as an emergent property (do not aim directly)
rubrics_metrics.description: Beauty may emerge from a completed plot but is not something the novelist should directly aim at; if he fails to achieve it he has failed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat beauty as a by-product: it should 'look a little surprised' rather than posed. The novelist should focus on convincing causality and construction; beauty will arise if those are well managed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance between character and plot
rubrics_metrics.description: There is an inherent tension: plot requires contributions from characters, but characters are large, shadowy, and sometimes resist being bent to plot demands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for incidents that spring out of character and react upon characters (Meredith's method) rather than plots that compel characters to suspend their natures (criticized in Hardy). If plot dominates too much, characters go 'dry and thin'; if characters dominate, the plot may fail to cohere. Know where the plot may legitimately demand a 'contribution' and where characters must be allowed freedom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surprise must be convincing and restorative
rubrics_metrics.description: A good plot causes surprise, and that surprise should be followed by a feeling of 'Oh, that's all right' — meaning the surprise fits and restores coherence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use shocks that arise plausibly from characters and circumstances (example: Meredith's horse‑whipping episode in Beauchamp's Career). Avoid surprises that merely shock without providing satisfying causal or emotional pay-off.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid contrived denouements and loss of character vitality at the end
rubrics_metrics.description: Many novels 'go off at the end' because the plot must be wound up; forced denouements often deaden characters and leave a book feeling wooden.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely reflexively on death or marriage to conclude; avoid authorial labor that substitutes mechanical closure for organic resolution. Preserve the life of characters through the ending and try to prevent the 'standstill while logic takes over from flesh and blood.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Planning vs organic growth of the novel
rubrics_metrics.description: Question whether a novel must be planned (plot-maker standing above the work) or may grow organically with the author thrown into it; both approaches are possible and have different effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Traditional plotting emphasizes cause-and-effect and controlled denouement; modern experiments (example: Gide's Les Faux Monnayeurs) attempt to replace or supplement the plot with diaries, fragments, or self-reflexive materials. Be aware of the trade-offs: planning can produce a polished plot, whereas growth can yield organic discovery but risks lack of cohesion.
